newsitem.title: GUAM: U.S. experts say no clue yet in cause of KAL crash.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts say no clue yet in cause of KAL crash.

text.p: The head of a team of U.S. air safety experts probing the crash of a Korean Airlines (KAL) jet in Guam said on Thursday it was too early to suggest a probable cause.
"It is really too early to speculate on the cause of this accident," said George Black, member of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and chairman of the team probing the crash.

The KAL Boeing 747, carrying 254 people from Seoul to Guam, crashed in torrential rain three miles (five km) from the airport early on Wednesday. There were 27 survivors and the remainder are feared dead.
Black also discounted speculation that the crash was somehow related to the absence of a key airport navigational device, called a glide scope indicator.
The device, which allows pilots to conduct smooth instrumental landings at night or in low-visibility weather, had been out of service at Guam's airport since July 8 for regular maintenance.
"That was fairly well-known information that the glide scope (indicator) was out," Black told a news conference at the U.S. Navy's communications headquarters in Guam.

In the absence of a glide scope indicator, pilots use radar beacons to determine the rough location of the plane in relation to the runway during approach and make a staircase-type descent towards a touchdown, instead of a smoother, gliding one.
Black said the plane's two "black boxes", the digital flight data and cockpit voice recorders, were in fair condition and were being analysed by the NTSB in Washington.
The two recorders are expected to shed light on the last moments of KAL Flight 801. The pilot did not report an emergency before his plane crashed into a hilly jungle area near the airport.

Black said his team of 18 experts would start a full investigation into the crash on Friday, after Thursday's preliminary survey of the crash site. He said his team would cover all aspects of the flight, including plane maintenance, weather and traffic conditions.

NTSB probes normally took more than a year to determine the cause of a crash, Black said. For example, he said, the final NTSB meeting on the May 1996 crash of a Valujet liner in Florida would be held later this month.
Black said information provided by the U.S. military, especially video footage and photographs of the crash, would speed up their probe.
"Certainly the U.S. Navy and others have provided us with meticulous photographs," Black said.
